analysis.one_liner: Lets agencies reclassify career federal policy staff and fire them without standard civil-service protections.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced in September 2023 with zero cosponsors, it sat in the House Oversight Committee until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would recreate "Schedule F," a job classification that moves career federal employees who work on policy — drafting rules, advising agency heads, handling non-public deliberations — out of the regular competitive civil service. Those employees would lose the standard lengthy removal procedures and, in many cases, union bargaining coverage, making it far easier for a president and agency heads to reassign or fire them. Supporters say this fixes weak performance management; critics say it lets an administration replace experienced career staff with loyalists.
analysis.who_benefits: The President, agency heads, and political appointees gain sweeping flexibility: they could reclassify tens of thousands of career policy positions at will and remove occupants without the multi-step due-process procedures that apply under current law. A new administration could also more easily place allies into jobs that today stay with career professionals across administrations.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs OPM to create a Schedule F in the excepted service for positions of a "confidential, policy-determining, policy-making, or policy-advocating character," and states that civil service removal rules "shall not apply" to those positions [S2].

It requires every agency head to review its workforce and petition OPM to move qualifying competitive-service positions into Schedule F, with particular attention to staff who draft regulations, supervise attorneys, handle deliberative material, or conduct union bargaining negotiations [S2].

Supporters argue this addresses a real problem the bill's own findings cite: federal surveys showing only about a quarter of federal employees think agencies handle poor performers effectively, and only a quarter of supervisors are confident they could remove one [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Career federal employees in policy-relevant jobs lose job-security protections they have held for decades: they could be fired or reassigned without the standard adverse-action procedures, and agencies are directed to petition to exclude Schedule F jobs from union bargaining units. Ordinary people bear an indirect risk — the expert, nonpartisan staff who administer Social Security benefits, approve drugs, enforce safety rules, and draft regulations could be replaced based on political loyalty rather than expertise, since the bill's definitions of covered positions are broad.
analysis.who_pays_short: Career federal employees in policy roles

drawbacks.text: The bill's definitions are sweeping: it directs agencies to consider moving any position with "substantive participation" in policy work or that works with deliberative material under a supervisor at GS-13 or above — language critics have said could cover a large share of the career workforce, converting thousands of protected jobs into at-will positions [S2].

Removing these employees from the competitive service makes it easier for each new administration to fill supposedly career jobs with political loyalists, weakening the nonpartisan civil service that keeps programs like benefit payments and drug approvals running the same way regardless of who holds the White House [S2].

The good-faith case for the bill is real but narrow: federal performance management is genuinely weak, and honest supporters would concede that the bill's answer — stripping due-process protections from an entire class of jobs — goes far beyond disciplining individual poor performers, who can already be removed under existing chapter 75 procedures that the bill eliminates for these positions [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The problem the bill targets — difficulty removing poor performers — is documented in the federal government's own surveys, so the impulse is legitimate. But the remedy is blunt: rather than fixing performance management, it removes long-standing job protections from an entire class of career positions whose coverage the bill itself defines expansively. The cost of a civil service that can be reshaped by loyalty tests falls not just on the affected employees but on everyone who depends on the government being run by experienced, nonpartisan professionals. On balance, the drawbacks outweigh the stated benefits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Oversight Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or markup, had no cosponsors, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. John James (R-MI) introduced the bill on September 5, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability the same day [S4].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired with the 118th Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Career federal employees kept their existing civil-service protections, because the bill drew no cosponsors and never moved out of committee. No group gained materially; the outcome was simply that the status quo held.

for.name: Rep. John James
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only supporter in the House; it had zero cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Oversight and Accountability
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing or markup was ever scheduled — letting the bill expire.

against.name: Federal employee unions (e.g., AFGE, NTEU)
against.what_they_did: Publicly campaigned against reviving Schedule F, which they argue would politicize the civil service and strip union bargaining rights; the bill directed agencies to petition to exclude Schedule F jobs from bargaining units.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded. The only sponsor was a Republican, no Democrat cosponsored it, and no bloc ever took a position on the bill itself on the record.

industries.note: The bill removes the core job protections of career employees in policy-relevant positions, letting agency heads remove them without standard adverse-action procedures. Its effect on the public runs through the workforce: the experienced staff who administer benefits, safety rules, and regulations could be swapped out for political reasons.

industries.industry: Presidents, agency heads, and political appointees
industries.note: The bill hands officeholders the power to reclassify career positions at will and replace their occupants, consolidating control of the executive workforce in political hands. That gain in incumbent power comes at the expense of the nonpartisan civil service the public relies on.
The bill directs agencies to petition the Federal Labor Relations Authority to exclude Schedule F positions from collective bargaining units, shrinking union coverage in the federal workforce.
